problem: Before this survey there was no up-to-date, comprehensive review of embodied AI. Earlier surveys predated the deep-learning era (2004–2006), and the only recent one ([11], Anderson et al. 2018) covered only the evaluation of embodied navigation. No survey jointly compared the many new 3D simulators or mapped which simulators support which research tasks.
motivation: The field is shifting from 'internet AI', which learns from curated datasets, to 'embodied AI', where agents learn from egocentric interaction. This shift has produced many simulators and tasks, and a researcher needs a structured way to pick a simulator for a given task. The authors organise the field along two axes: simulator features (realism, scalability, interactivity) and a task 'pyramid' of increasing complexity: visual exploration → visual navigation → embodied QA.
key_idea: Benchmark nine embodied-AI simulators (drawn from the CVPR Embodied AI workshop challenges) on seven technical features grouped into realism / scalability / interactivity. Then survey the three core tasks built on them (exploration, navigation, embodied QA) as a hierarchical pyramid, and link simulators, datasets and tasks.
insight: Simulators that score on all three secondary features are the most widely adopted: AI2-THOR, iGibson and Habitat-Sim. Habitat-Sim (10,000 fps/thread) and iGibson (1000 fps/thread) lead in rendering speed, and they are the only world-based (real-scan) simulators, which the authors argue matters most for sim-to-real. Interactive tasks such as EQA/IQA and navigation with priors require multi-state objects, which favours AI2-THOR. VLN at the time used none of the nine simulators, only the Matterport3D Simulator, because it needed no interactivity. On the research side, memory/representation (RNN vs. attention vs. occupancy/semantic maps) is identified as central but unresolved for lack of dedicated comparisons. Hybrid classic+learned methods (e.g., Active Neural SLAM) and prior-knowledge injection are highlighted as the main routes to lower sample complexity.
method: Simulator selection: nine simulators (DeepMind Lab, AI2-THOR, CHALET, VirtualHome, VRKitchen, Habitat-Sim, iGibson, SAPIEN, ThreeDWorld) taken from the CVPR Embodied AI workshop challenges; research tasks sourced from papers citing these simulators.

Seven primary features (Table I): Environment (game-based G vs world-based W); Physics (basic B vs advanced A: cloth/fluid/soft-body); Object Type (dataset-driven D vs asset-driven O); Object Property (interactable I, multi-state M); Controller (Python API P, virtual robot R, VR V); Action (navigation N, atomic A, human-computer interaction H); Multi-agent (avatar-based AT, user-based U).

Three secondary features: realism (environment + physics), scalability (object type) and interactivity (object property, controller, action, multi-agent). Plus a quantitative comparison (Table II) of environment configuration, engine, hardware and rendering fps/thread.

Task pyramid (Table III, Fig. 5): visual exploration (curiosity, coverage, reconstruction), visual navigation (PointNav, ObjectNav, navigation with priors, VLN, vision-dialog navigation), and embodied QA (EQA, MT-EQA, IQA, multi-agent IQA). For each task it reviews approaches, evaluation metrics and datasets.
Simulator–task–dataset connection graph (Fig. 6), plus a proposed next pyramid level, Task-based Interactive QA (TIQA), in which the agent must perform tasks to obtain the answer.

Challenges analysis: simulators (realism, scalability of 3D scan collection, interactivity trade-off between symbolic and fine-grained manipulation) and research (memory architectures, compounding task complexity, hard ablations, neglect of multi-agent set-ups).

setting.observation: n/a (surveys methods using egocentric RGB / RGB-D, GPS+compass for PointNav, language for VLN/EQA)
setting.simulator: surveys DeepMind Lab, AI2-THOR, CHALET, VirtualHome, VRKitchen, Habitat-Sim, iGibson, SAPIEN, ThreeDWorld (plus Matterport3D Simulator and House3D for VLN/EQA)

numbers_note: Survey paper: it reports no experimental results of its own. Table II lists simulator rendering throughput as quoted from the original simulator papers (e.g., Habitat-Sim 10,000 fps/thread, iGibson 1000 fps/thread, AI2-THOR 240 fps/thread). Table III lists which metrics each surveyed method uses, but no benchmark scores.
results: No new experimental results. The comparison concludes that AI2-THOR, iGibson and Habitat-Sim cover all three of realism, scalability and interactivity and are the most widely used: AI2-THOR has the largest environment configuration (120 rooms), and Habitat-Sim and iGibson lead rendering performance. Only Habitat-Sim and iGibson are world-based, and only ThreeDWorld has advanced physics, which the authors flag as a key gap. Habitat-Sim/iGibson suit exploration and navigation, AI2-THOR suits interactive QA and navigation with priors, and VLN then relied on the Matterport3D Simulator.
limitations: Coverage is narrow and quickly dated: only nine simulators (early 2021 snapshot), and VLN is covered by just three papers (Seq2Seq, AuxRN, CMN). Omitted are the Matterport3D Simulator as a surveyed platform, VLN-CE, REVERIE, RxR, HM3D-based benchmarks and later transformer/LLM-based methods.
No quantitative comparison of methods on benchmarks: it gives feature and metric tables but no SR/SPL results tables, so it cannot guide method selection by performance.
Excludes Sim2Real and physical robotics. Some feature assignments are coarse or debatable, e.g., Habitat-Sim is listed with no physics, controller or object property.
